title: Check yourself: shared and thread-local memory

questions.stem: A validator collects bad file names with `List<String> errors = new ArrayList<>(); files.parallelStream().forEach(f -> { if (!valid(f)) errors.add(f); }); return errors;`. The stream runs the lambda on several threads. Is `errors` safe to use this way?

options.text: Safe, since errors is a local variable, and a local is never shared between threads
options.says: the variable is private, but the ArrayList it refers to is on the heap and every thread running the lambda reaches it

options.text: Safe, since the lambda captures errors by value, so each thread works on a copy of the list
options.says: capturing copies the value of the local, which is a reference; every copy points to the same list

options.text: Unsafe, since the threads running the lambda all add to the one list that errors refers to
options.says: the captured reference points to one ArrayList on the heap, which several threads modify at once

options.text: Unsafe, since errors lives in the calling thread's frame, which the stream's other threads cannot read
options.says: the other threads never read the caller's frame; they get a copy of the reference, and the problem is the shared list it points to

origin.section: Fields, Statics and Array Elements Are Shared; Locals and Parameters Are Not

questions.stem: On an x86 server, a status thread runs `while (!ready) { checks++; }` over a plain boolean field. Minutes later another thread sets `ready = true`, and the loop never ends. Which explanation fits?

options.text: The reader's cache holds the old value, since a read is served from the core's own cache until the line is evicted
options.says: caches are coherent: a core reading the address sees the latest store that reached any cache

options.text: The writer's cache holds the new value, since a write leaves the core only when a fence flushes it
options.says: coherence delivers plain writes without any fence; the opaque loop saw a plain write within a fraction of a millisecond

options.text: The reader's register holds the old value, since the compiled code loaded the field once and never read it again
options.says: the JIT may read a plain field once and keep it in a register; the same loop with opaque reads ended within a fraction of a millisecond

options.text: The writer's store buffer holds the new value, since a store leaves the buffer only when a fence drains it
options.says: a store buffer holds a write only briefly and drains to the cache on its own, no fence needed; it can reorder, not hide a write

origin.section: Threads Don't Keep Private Copies of Memory; Compiled Code Keeps Values in Registers

questions.stem: A web app keeps each request's locale in an InheritableThreadLocal. Reports run on `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)`, created at startup and unused until the first report. The first four reports, all submitted while others were still running, came from a German user and three French users. Later an English user submits a report. In which locale does it come out?

options.text: English, since each submit copies the submitting thread's inheritable values into the task
options.says: the copy happens when a thread is created, not when a task is submitted

options.text: English, since the task's get() reads the value of the thread that submitted the task
options.says: get() reads the current thread's own value, here the pool thread's

options.text: German or French, since each pool thread kept the value it copied from the request that started it
options.says: the pool's threads were created inside the first four submits and copied those requests' values once

options.text: No locale, since inheritable values are copied only into threads created with new Thread, not into pool threads
options.says: a pool creates its threads inside submit, on the submitting thread, so they inherit like any other child thread

origin.section: InheritableThreadLocal Copies the Value Once, When a Thread Is Created

questions.stem: Eight worker threads count events in a shared `AtomicLongArray(8)`; worker i only ever updates slot i. On a 16-core machine, eight workers count fewer events per second in total than one worker alone. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The slots share cache lines, since neighbouring longs sit in one line that each write takes from the other cores
options.says: coherence works on cache lines: cores writing different variables in one line pass the line back and forth

options.text: The slots share a lock, since an AtomicLongArray update holds one monitor for the whole array while it runs
options.says: the atomic classes are lock-free; the slots share no lock, only cache lines

options.text: The workers contend on nothing, since each slot has one writer, so the slowdown must come from somewhere else
options.says: separate variables in one cache line still contend, as the adjacent-fields run showed

options.text: The workers contend on the array reference, since every update first reads the field that holds the array
options.says: a line that is only read sits in every core's cache at once; the writes to neighbouring slots are what move lines

origin.section: Threads That Share No Variable Can Still Share a Cache Line
